title: Java Programming with IntelliJ IDEA
subtitle: Write, test and debug object-oriented Java in IntelliJ IDEA, from your first Maven project to a tested command-line application.
outcomes: Set up a JDK and a Maven project in IntelliJ IDEA, and build and run Java programs from the IDE
Write Java with variables, types, decisions, loops and methods
Model problems with classes, constructors, inheritance, interfaces and records
Process data with lists, sets, maps and streams, and handle errors with exceptions
Test code with JUnit 5 and find bugs with IntelliJ IDEA's debugger
prerequisites: None: this course starts from zero. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer that can run IntelliJ IDEA (the free version is enough) and an internet connection: IntelliJ IDEA downloads a JDK for you, and the Maven that comes with it downloads the libraries your projects use.
description: Learn Java the way professional developers write it: in IntelliJ IDEA, an IDE that understands your code. Each lesson teaches a Java idea and then shows it in IntelliJ IDEA, step by step, with the keyboard shortcuts for macOS, Windows and Linux, so you learn the language and the tool together. You'll create a Maven project with a JDK the IDE downloads for you and write programs with types, decisions, loops and methods. Then you'll model real things with classes, inheritance, interfaces and records, process data with collections and streams, and handle what goes wrong with exceptions. Finally you'll prove your code works with JUnit 5 tests and track bugs down with the debugger instead of guesswork. Every module ends with a hands-on lab that you do in IntelliJ IDEA and submit for your instructor's feedback, and the course ends with a library-management app that you build from scratch.

modules.title: Get set up and write your first programs
modules.summary: Create a Maven project in IntelliJ IDEA with a JDK it downloads for you, then write programs with Java's types, decisions, loops and methods, with an editor that completes and checks your code as you type.

lessons.title: How Java runs, and your first Maven project
objectives: Explain what the JDK, the JVM and bytecode are
Create a Maven project in IntelliJ IDEA with a JDK it downloads for you
Write, run and configure a program with a main method
key_points: The compiler, javac, turns .java source files into bytecode in .class files, and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs that bytecode, so the same compiled program runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

The JDK (Java Development Kit) holds the compiler, the JVM and the standard library. Several vendors build it from the open-source OpenJDK project, and any of them works; this course needs Java 21 or later.
Maven builds a project from its pom.xml file, which names the project with coordinates (a groupId such as org.example, an artifactId and a version) and lists the libraries it depends on.
Maven expects source code in src/main/java and tests in src/test/java, and writes what it builds to the target folder; its package phase compiles the code, runs the tests and makes a .jar file.

A program starts in public static void main(String[] args). A public class lives in a file with the same name, and a package statement, such as package org.example;, matches the folder the file is in.
A run configuration remembers how to run a class: its main class, its program arguments and its JDK. IntelliJ IDEA makes one the first time you run a class.

walkthrough.title: Create a Maven project and run a program

steps.do: On the Welcome screen click New Project. Choose Java as the language and Maven as the build system, name the project java-basics and tick Add sample code.

Open the JDK list and choose Download JDK. Pick version 21 or later and any vendor, such as Eclipse Temurin or Oracle OpenJDK, and click Download. Then open Advanced Settings, set GroupId to org.example and click Create.
steps.see: The project opens with a pom.xml file and a src folder, while the JDK downloads in the background.

steps.do: Open pom.xml. Find the project's coordinates (groupId, artifactId and version) and the properties maven.compiler.source and maven.compiler.target, which set the Java version the code is compiled for.
In the Project tool window, select the org.example package under src/main/java and create a Java class named Greeter.
Inside the class, type main and press Enter to insert a main method (psvm works too). Inside it, type sout and press Enter for System.out.println(). Finish the code.
Run Greeter with the green arrow beside its main method in the gutter, or with the caret inside it.
steps.see: Hello, world! in the Run tool window, then Process finished with exit code 0.

steps.do: Open Run | Edit Configurations, select Greeter, type Amara in Program arguments and click OK. Then rerun the last configuration.
steps.see: Hello, Amara!

steps.do: With Greeter.java open, choose View | Show Bytecode to see what the compiler made from it: the instructions the JVM runs.
steps.see: Instructions in capitals, such as GETSTATIC, LDC and INVOKEVIRTUAL.

steps.do: Open the Maven tool window (View | Tool Windows | Maven) and double-click java-basics | Lifecycle | package.
steps.see: BUILD SUCCESS in the Run tool window, and a java-basics-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar file in the target folder.

steps.do: Run any Maven command by name with Run Anything: press Ctrl twice and type mvn clean package. It uses the Maven that comes with IntelliJ IDEA, so there's nothing else to install.

lessons.title: Variables, types and strings
objectives: Choose between Java's primitive types and String
Avoid integer-division and string-comparison mistakes
Let completion, quick-fixes and documentation help you write code
key_points: Java is statically typed: a variable's type is fixed when it's declared, as in int count = 3;, and the compiler rejects code that uses a value of the wrong type.
The primitive types include int and long for whole numbers, double for decimals, boolean for true or false and char for a single character; String, for text, is a class.
Dividing two ints gives an int and drops the remainder: 7 / 2 is 3. Make one side a double, as in 7 / 2.0, to get 3.5; % gives the remainder, so 7 % 2 is 1.
var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type from its value: var total = 0; declares an int. The type is still fixed; it just isn't written out.

Compare strings with equals, not ==, which only checks whether two references point to the same object. Integer.parseInt("42") turns text into an int and throws NumberFormatException for text that isn't a number.

String.format and printf format values for display: String.format("%.2f", 3.14159) gives 3.14. They follow the computer's locale, so pass Locale.ROOT first to get a dot as the decimal separator everywhere.

walkthrough.title: Let the editor help with types

steps.do: Create a class TypesDemo with a main method and try integer division.
steps.see: 3 and 3.5 when you run it.

steps.do: Add the line int half = exact / 2; and see it underlined in red: a double can't be stored in an int without a cast. Put the caret on it, open Show Context Actions and choose the fix that casts the value to int.
steps.see: (int) is added in front of the expression.

steps.do: Type the line below, letting completion fill in names such as format and Locale. Choosing Locale from the list also adds import java.util.Locale; at the top of the file.
steps.code: System.out.println(String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", exact));
steps.see: 3.50 when you run it.

steps.do: Put the caret inside format's brackets to see the parameters it takes.
Put the caret on format and read its documentation without leaving the editor.
Compare two strings with ==. IntelliJ IDEA highlights the comparison, and Show Context Actions offers to replace it with equals().
Put the caret on var in a declaration such as var count = 3; and open Show Context Actions: it offers to replace var with the explicit type. On an explicit type, it offers the opposite.

lessons.title: Decisions, loops and methods
objectives: Choose between actions with if and switch
Repeat work with for, for-each and while loops over arrays
Write static methods with parameters and return values
key_points: if and else run a block only when a condition is true. Conditions compare with ==, !=, <, <=, > and >=, and combine with && (and), || (or) and ! (not).
A switch expression picks a value: String kind = switch (day) { case "Sat", "Sun" -> "weekend"; default -> "weekday"; }; arrow cases don't fall through to the next case.

An array holds a fixed number of values of one type: int[] steps = {4200, 9800}; steps[0] is the first and steps.length is 2. for (int i = 0; i < steps.length; i++) visits each index, and for (int s : steps) each value.
while repeats as long as its condition is true; break leaves a loop at once, and continue skips to the loop's next round.
A method has a return type, a name and parameters, as in static double average(int[] values). return gives back its result, and a void method returns nothing.
Java passes arguments by value: a method gets a copy of each primitive, and a copy of the reference for an object, so reassigning a parameter never changes the caller's variable.

steps.do: Inside main, type fori and press Enter to insert a counting for loop. Press Tab to move between the parts you fill in.
steps.see: for (int i = 0; i < ; i++) with the caret where the limit goes.

steps.do: Below an array, type iter and press Enter: IntelliJ IDEA writes a for-each loop over it.
Select a line and wrap it in an if, a loop or a try block with Surround With.
Write an old-style switch statement with case and break, put the caret on switch and open Show Context Actions: IntelliJ IDEA offers to replace it with an enhanced switch.
Select the lines that add up the array and extract them into a method.
steps.see: A new static method, and a call to it where the lines were.

steps.do: Rename the new method to total: every call to it is updated.
Type /** on the line above the method and press Enter: IntelliJ IDEA writes a Javadoc comment with @param and @return tags to fill in. Then read it from a call to the method.

lab.title: Write a step-count report
lab.goal: Finish a program that reports a week of step counts: each day's activity level, the total, the daily average, the best day and the weekend's steps, in a Maven project that builds.
setup: IntelliJ IDEA (the free version is enough)
The java-basics Maven project from the lesson, with a JDK of version 21 or later
The starter file StepReport.java, which goes in src/main/java/org/example

steps.do: If you haven't yet, create the java-basics project: Java, the Maven build system, GroupId org.example and a JDK of version 21 or later. Put StepReport.java in src/main/java/org/example.
Open StepReport.java, and the TODO tool window (View | Tool Windows | TODO) to see every TODO in one list.
Write total and average. average must divide as a double: (double) total(values) / values.length.
Write indexOfMax, then level with if, else if and else, then isWeekend with a switch expression.
Write main: loop over the days by index, print each day's line and add up the weekend's steps with isWeekend, then print the four summary lines.
Run StepReport.

steps.do: Reformat the file, then fix anything IntelliJ IDEA still highlights; F2 jumps from one problem to the next.
Build the project with Maven: in the Maven tool window, double-click Lifecycle | package.

checks.text: Each day's count and activity level are right.
The total and the average are right: the average isn't cut short by integer division.
The best day is found by indexOfMax, not written in by hand.

The project builds with Maven.

Keep the index of the best day, not just its count, so you can print its name from DAYS.

modules.title: Object-oriented programming
modules.summary: Model the things a program works with as objects: classes with private fields and constructors, inheritance and polymorphism, interfaces, and records for plain data, with IntelliJ IDEA generating the routine code.

lessons.title: Classes, objects and constructors
objectives: Write a class with private fields, a constructor and methods
Generate constructors, getters and toString with IntelliJ IDEA
key_points: A class is a blueprint and an object is one instance of it: new Light("Hall light") calls a constructor and creates a Light object.
Fields hold an object's state and methods its behaviour. Making fields private and changing them only through methods (encapsulation) lets the class keep its state valid.
A constructor has the class's name and no return type; this.name = name; assigns the parameter to the field of the same name. A class can have several constructors with different parameters.
A constructor or method rejects bad input by throwing an exception, as in throw new IllegalArgumentException("level must be between 0 and 100");
static members belong to the class rather than to each object, and a final field can be assigned only once, usually in the constructor.
Every class extends Object, whose toString() is used when an object is printed; overriding it gives readable output instead of something like Light@1b6d3586.

steps.do: In the Project tool window, select src/main/java/org/example and create a Java class. Type home.Light as its name: IntelliJ IDEA creates the home package and the class in it.
Type two fields.
steps.code:
private final String name;
private int level;

steps.do: Open Generate inside the class, choose Constructor and select name.
steps.see: A constructor that sets this.name = name.

steps.do: Open Generate again, choose Getter and select both fields; then open it once more and choose toString().
Add a method that changes the state only when the new value is valid.
See the class's fields, constructor and methods in one popup.
In a class with a main method, create a Light and type a dot after the variable's name: completion lists only what Light makes public. Run it.
steps.see: Light{name='Hall light', level=60}

lessons.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
objectives: Extend a class and override its methods
Explain polymorphism and abstract classes
Navigate a class hierarchy in IntelliJ IDEA
key_points: A subclass extends one superclass, as in class Thermostat extends Device, and inherits its fields and methods; its constructor calls super(...) first to set up the inherited part.
A subclass can override a method to change its behaviour; the @Override annotation asks the compiler to check that the method really overrides one in the superclass.
An abstract class can't be instantiated and may declare abstract methods, without a body, that every concrete subclass must implement.
Polymorphism: a variable of type Device can refer to a Light or a Thermostat, and calling status() on it runs the version belonging to the object's actual class.
protected members are visible to subclasses and to classes in the same package; a final class can't be extended, and a final method can't be overridden.
Inheritance suits an is-a relationship: a thermostat is a device. When one class merely uses another, give it a field of that type instead, which is called composition.

steps.do: Create an abstract class Device in the home package.
Create a class Thermostat and add extends Device. It's underlined in red: open Show Context Actions and choose Create constructor matching super, then Implement methods.
steps.see: A constructor that calls super(name), and a status() method to fill in.

steps.do: Fill in status(), then override toString() with Generate | Override Methods.
Put the caret on the abstract status() in Device and jump to the classes that implement it.
With the caret on Device, choose Navigate | Type Hierarchy to see the whole tree of classes.
Click the icon beside an overriding method in the gutter to jump to the method it overrides in the superclass.
When two subclasses share a method, move it into the superclass: open Refactor This on the method and choose Pull Members Up.

lessons.title: Interfaces and records
objectives: Define and implement interfaces, including default methods
Use records for immutable data, with validation in a compact constructor
key_points: An interface declares what a type can do without saying how, as in interface Dimmable { void setLevel(int level); }; a class that implements it must provide those methods.
A class extends only one class but can implement several interfaces, which is how Java shares a capability across unrelated classes.
An interface can have default methods with a body; classes that implement the interface inherit them unless they override them.
A record is a short way to write an immutable data class: record Reading(String device, double value) {} gets a constructor, the accessors device() and value(), and equals, hashCode and toString.
A record's compact constructor validates the arguments before the fields are set: public Reading { if (device.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a reading needs a device"); }
Records can implement interfaces but can't extend other classes, and their fields are final: to change a value, create a new record.

walkthrough.title: Interfaces and records in the IDE

steps.do: Create an interface: open New in the Project tool window, choose Java Class, type Dimmable and pick Interface in the list.
Add implements Dimmable to Light. If a method is missing, open Show Context Actions on the red underline and choose Implement methods.
Create a record: New | Java Class, type Reading and pick Record.
steps.code:
public record Reading(String device, double value) {
}

steps.do: Use the record: completion lists the accessors device() and value() that Java generated. Run it.
steps.see: Reading[device=Lounge thermostat, value=19.5] and then 19.5

steps.do: Add a compact constructor that rejects a blank device name.
On an ordinary class that only holds final fields, put the caret on the class name and open Show Context Actions: IntelliJ IDEA can offer to convert it to a record.

lab.title: Model a smart home
lab.goal: Model a smart home's devices with an abstract class, two subclasses, an interface with a default method and a record, then print every device's status through one array of Device.
setup: Your java-basics project, or any Maven project with a JDK of version 21 or later
The starter files Device.java, Dimmable.java and SmartHome.java, which go in src/main/java/org/example/home. You write Light, Thermostat and Reading.

steps.do: Copy the starter files into src/main/java/org/example/home and open SmartHome.java. It's full of red: Light, Thermostat and Reading don't exist yet.
Put the caret on Light, open Show Context Actions and choose Create class 'Light'. Make it extend Device and implement Dimmable.

Write Light: a constructor that passes the name to super, a level from 0 to 100 (setLevel throws IllegalArgumentException("level must be between 0 and 100") for anything else), getLevel, and status(), which returns Hall light: on at 60% or Hall light: off.

Write Thermostat, extending Device: setTarget(double) accepts 5 to 30 and otherwise throws IllegalArgumentException("target must be between 5 and 30"); status() returns Lounge thermostat: on, target 21.5 degrees or Lounge thermostat: off.
Create Reading as a record with a String device and a double value, and a compact constructor that throws IllegalArgumentException("a reading needs a device") for a blank device.
Run SmartHome.
steps.see: Four status lines, then Reading[device=Lounge thermostat, value=19.5], then three lines that start with Rejected:

steps.do: Put a breakpoint on the line in the for loop that prints device.status().
Debug SmartHome, then step into status() each time round the loop: each object runs its own class's version.
Reformat each file you wrote.

checks.text: Every device reports its own status through the Device array.
Dimmable's default brighten method caps the level at 100.
Reading is a record, printed by the toString that Java generated for it.
Bad values are rejected with exceptions from the setters and from the record's compact constructor.
look_for: Rejected: level must be between 0 and 100
Rejected: target must be between 5 and 30
Rejected: a reading needs a device

checks.text: Light and Thermostat extend Device, and Light implements Dimmable.

lab.submit: Paste Light.java, Thermostat.java and Reading.java, then the output of SmartHome from the Run tool window.

status() can use isOn() and getName(), which Light and Thermostat inherit from Device.
Methods that implement an interface's methods must be public.

modules.title: Collections, streams and exceptions
modules.summary: Store and look up data with lists, sets and maps, process it with streams and lambdas, and handle what goes wrong, from a bad line of input to a missing file, with exceptions.

lessons.title: Lists, sets and maps
objectives: Choose between List, Set and Map
Use generics, and IntelliJ IDEA's postfix completion, to work with collections
key_points: A List keeps elements in order and allows duplicates: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); names.add("Amara"); names.get(0) is the first element and names.size() the number of elements.
A Set holds each element at most once, and a Map stores values by key: after stock.put("tea", 12), stock.get("tea") is 12, and get returns null for a key that isn't there.
The type in angle brackets is a type argument: a List<String> can hold only strings, so mistakes are caught when compiling. Collections hold objects, so int values are stored as Integer.
List.of, Set.of and Map.of create unmodifiable collections; calling add or put on one throws UnsupportedOperationException.
map.getOrDefault(key, 0) avoids null for a missing key, and map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) counts occurrences in one line.
HashMap and HashSet keep no particular order, while TreeMap and TreeSet keep their keys sorted; they all rely on equals and hashCode, which String and records provide.

walkthrough.title: Work with collections in the editor

steps.do: Type List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); and choose ArrayList from the completion list, which adds its import. If a name stays red, open Show Context Actions on it and choose Import class.
Try postfix completion: type names.for and choose for from the completion list to turn it into a for-each loop; names.size().sout wraps the value in System.out.println.
Count words with a TreeMap and merge, then run the code.
steps.see: {cat=1, dog=1, saw=1, the=2}

steps.do: Put the caret on merge and read its documentation.
Toggle a breakpoint on the println line.
Debug the program and expand counts in the Debug tool window's Variables pane: a map's entries are shown as key and value pairs.
Call add on a list made with List.of("a", "b") and run it: the Run tool window shows the exception, with a link to the line that caused it.
steps.see: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

lessons.title: Streams and lambdas
objectives: Write lambdas and method references
Filter, transform, group and summarise data with streams
Turn loops into streams, and trace streams, with IntelliJ IDEA
key_points: A lambda is a short anonymous function, such as s -> s.length() or (a, b) -> a + b; a method reference, such as String::toUpperCase, names an existing method instead.

A stream is a pipeline over a collection's elements: list.stream(), then intermediate operations such as filter, map and sorted, then one terminal operation, such as toList(), count() or forEach, that produces the result.
Streams don't change the collection they read from, and nothing runs until the terminal operation is called.
Collectors.groupingBy(Observation::city, Collectors.averagingDouble(Observation::tempC)) groups elements by a key and summarises each group, giving a Map.
max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Observation::tempC)) finds the largest element and returns an Optional, which is empty when there are no elements; orElseThrow() gets the value out.
IntelliJ IDEA can replace many loops with streams through Show Context Actions, and its debugger can trace a stream to show what each step did.

steps.do: Write a loop that collects the long words, in upper case, into a new list. Put the caret on for, open Show Context Actions and choose the option that replaces the loop with the Stream API.
steps.see: A stream with filter and map in place of the loop.

steps.do: Where the stream has a lambda such as w -> w.toUpperCase(), open Show Context Actions on it: IntelliJ IDEA offers to replace it with the method reference String::toUpperCase.
Group the words by length and count each group, then run the code.
Put the caret inside groupingBy's brackets to see its forms: with a key function only, with a downstream collector, and with a map factory as well.
Toggle a breakpoint on the line where the stream starts.
Debug the program. When it stops at the breakpoint, open Find Action and run Trace Current Stream Chain.
steps.see: A window with a tab for each operation, showing the elements that went into it and came out.

lessons.title: Exceptions and files
objectives: Explain checked and unchecked exceptions
Catch exceptions, and close resources with try-with-resources
Read a text file with java.nio.file
key_points: An exception signals that something went wrong; if nothing catches it, the program stops and prints a stack trace that names the exception and the line where it was thrown.
try { ... } catch (NumberFormatException e) { ... } handles one kind of exception, catch (A | B e) handles two, and a finally block runs whether or not an exception was thrown.
Checked exceptions, such as IOException, must be caught or declared with throws in the method's signature; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException, such as IllegalArgumentException, and needn't be.
Files.readAllLines(Path.of("readings.csv")) reads a whole text file, as UTF-8, into a List<String>; it throws NoSuchFileException, a kind of IOException, when the file doesn't exist.
try-with-resources, as in try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { ... }, closes the resource for you, even when an exception is thrown.
Catch an exception only where you can do something useful about it, such as skipping a bad line or showing a message; an empty catch block hides bugs.

walkthrough.title: Handle exceptions with the IDE's help

steps.do: In main, call Files.readAllLines(Path.of("readings.csv")). The call is underlined in red because IOException isn't handled. Put the caret on it and open Show Context Actions.
steps.see: Fixes that add the exception to the method's signature or surround the call with try/catch.

steps.do: Choose Surround with try/catch, or select the lines and use Surround With, and finish the code.
Run it before readings.csv exists. Then create the file in the project's top-level folder, which is the run configuration's working directory, add a few lines and run it again.
steps.see: Could not read the file: java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: readings.csv, and then a line count once the file is there.

steps.do: Call Integer.parseInt("abc") outside any try block and run it. In the stack trace, click the link to your own file to jump to the line that failed.
steps.see: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"

steps.do: Add an exception breakpoint that stops wherever a NumberFormatException is thrown: open View Breakpoints, click +, choose Java Exception Breakpoints and type NumberFormatException.
Debug the program. It stops where the exception is thrown, inside the JDK's parsing code, and the Frames list shows the calls that led there from your main method.

lab.title: Analyse weather readings
lab.goal: Read a CSV file of weather readings into records, skipping and counting the lines that can't be parsed, then report each city's average temperature, the hottest reading and the number of rainy readings with streams.

modules.title: Testing with JUnit 5 and debugging
modules.summary: Prove your code works with JUnit 5 tests that run in IntelliJ IDEA and in Maven, cover many cases with parameterised tests, measure coverage, and find bugs with the debugger instead of guesswork.

lessons.title: Unit tests with JUnit 5
objectives: Add JUnit 5 to a Maven project
Write tests with @Test and assertions
Create, run and rerun tests in IntelliJ IDEA
key_points: A unit test checks that a small piece of code, such as one method, gives the result you expect. JUnit 5 is a widely used testing framework for Java; the way you write tests with it is called JUnit Jupiter.
The junit-jupiter dependency, with <scope>test</scope> in pom.xml, adds JUnit 5 to a Maven project. Test classes go in src/test/java, usually in the same package as the class they test.

A test is a method annotated with @Test. Assertions say what must be true: assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue(condition) and assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> checker.problems(null)).
@BeforeEach marks a method that runs before every test, so each test starts with fresh objects and doesn't depend on the others.
Maven's test phase runs every test, using the Surefire plugin, and the build fails if a test fails. Surefire versions before 2.22 don't find JUnit 5 tests, so pom.xml should name a recent one.

steps.do: Add JUnit 5 and a recent Surefire plugin to pom.xml, inside <project>, then click the Load Maven Changes button that appears in the editor.
steps.code:
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
        <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
        <version>5.11.4</version>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.5.2</version>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

lessons.title: Parameterised tests and coverage
objectives: Run one test with many inputs using @ParameterizedTest
Measure which code your tests run with coverage
key_points: @ParameterizedTest runs one test method once for each set of arguments, so many inputs can be checked without copying the test.
@ValueSource(ints = {0, 1, 4999}) supplies single values, and @CsvSource({"4999, low", "5000, moderate"}) supplies rows of several arguments, converted to the parameters' types.
Parameterised tests come from junit-jupiter-params, which the junit-jupiter dependency already includes.
Good tests check the boundaries of each rule, such as 4999 and 5000 steps, and invalid input, as well as typical values.
assertAll(...) runs a group of assertions and reports every failure in the group, not just the first one.
Coverage shows which lines your tests ran. A line that no test runs is untested, but full coverage doesn't prove the code is right.

steps.do: Replace the single level test with a parameterised test.
If ParameterizedTest or CsvSource is red, put the caret on it and open Show Context Actions to add the import.
Run the test class.
steps.see: Five runs under levelMatchesTheStepCount, numbered [1] to [5], each with its arguments.

steps.do: Open the menu on the green arrow beside the class name and choose Run with Coverage.
steps.see: The Coverage tool window shows the percentage of classes, methods and lines covered, and marks in the editor's gutter show which lines ran.

steps.do: Open StepReport.java and find a line that no test ran. Write a test that runs it, such as one for isWeekend, and run with coverage again.

lessons.title: Debugging Java in IntelliJ IDEA
objectives: Pause a program or a test at a breakpoint and step through it
Inspect state with the Variables pane, watches and Evaluate Expression
Use conditional breakpoints to stop only when something interesting happens
key_points: A breakpoint pauses the program at a line so you can look at its state; you can debug a main method or a single failing test in the same way.
Step Over runs the current line and stops at the next, Step Into goes inside the method the line calls, and Step Out finishes the current method and returns to its caller.
While the program is paused, the Variables pane shows every variable in scope, including the fields of this, and the Frames list shows the chain of method calls that led to the current line.
Evaluate Expression runs any Java expression in the paused program, such as password.charAt(0), and a watch keeps an expression in view as you step.
A conditional breakpoint stops only when its condition is true, such as i == 6 in a long loop; Run to Cursor runs to the caret's line without a permanent breakpoint.

steps.do: Toggle a breakpoint on the first line of the method that a failing test calls.
steps.see: A red dot in the gutter.

steps.do: Click the green arrow beside the failing test method and choose Debug.
steps.see: The test stops at your breakpoint, and the Debug tool window opens.

steps.do: Step over a line at a time and watch the Variables pane change.
Step into a method that the current line calls.
Step out of it, back to the caller.
Evaluate an expression in the paused program.

steps.do: Right-click a breakpoint's red dot and type a condition, so that it only stops when the condition is true.
Put the caret on a later line and run to it.
Resume the program until the next breakpoint, or the end.

project.title: Build a library-management command-line app
project.brief: Build a command-line app in IntelliJ IDEA that a small community library could use for its books and loans. Librarians can add books (ISBN, title, author and year), register members, lend a book to a member for 14 days, take it back, search by title or author, and list the loans that are overdue on a given date. Model books, members and loans with classes and records, keep them in collections, and use streams for searching and reporting. Report problems, such as an unknown ISBN or a book that's already on loan, with your own exceptions, so the app prints a clear message and carries on. Save the data to a file so it's still there next time. Build it as a Maven project, test it with JUnit 5, and use the debugger whenever something doesn't behave.
deliverables: A Maven project, pom.xml and the source code, with at least one record, one interface or abstract class, and one exception class of your own
A command loop that reads commands (such as add, member, lend, return, search, overdue and quit) and prints clear results
Saving and loading the books, members and loans, with a friendly message when the data file is missing
At least eight JUnit 5 tests, including a parameterised test and tests that expect exceptions
A README.md that explains how to build, run and test the app
The output of a session that adds, lends, returns and searches, and lists overdue loans, plus the summary of mvn test

rubric.name: It works
rubric.description: Every command works: books and members can be added, books lent and returned, searches find matches by title or author, and overdue loans are listed correctly for a given date.

rubric.name: Object-oriented design
rubric.description: Classes, records and interfaces model the library sensibly, with private fields, validated constructors and methods that each do one thing.

rubric.name: Collections and streams
rubric.description: Suitable collections, such as a Map from ISBN to book, and streams for searching and reporting where they read better than loops.

rubric.name: Error handling
rubric.description: Unknown ISBNs, books already on loan, bad dates and a missing data file give clear messages through custom exceptions; the app never ends with a stack trace.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: At least eight meaningful JUnit 5 tests that cover normal cases, edge cases and expected exceptions, all passing in mvn test.

rubric.name: Readability and README
rubric.description: Consistent formatting, clear names, and a README that explains how to build, run and test the app.

project.submit: Paste your code (each file with its path), your tests, your README, the output of a session and the summary of mvn test. A link to a public repository is welcome too.
